lesson.title: continue: Skipping Ahead to the Next Iteration
lesson.summary: The continue statement skips the rest of the current pass through a loop and jumps straight to the next one, without ending the loop the way break does.
lesson.body:
The continue statement is often introduced alongside break because both interrupt a loop's normal top-to-bottom flow, but they do genuinely different things. break ends the loop entirely, with no more passes at all. continue does something gentler: it stops executing the remaining lines of the current pass and immediately moves on to the next one, re-checking a while loop's condition or advancing a for loop to its next item, exactly as if that particular pass had simply reached the bottom of the body naturally on its own.

This is useful whenever you want to skip certain items while still processing all the rest, rather than stopping the whole loop altogether. Consider:
numbers = [3, -1, 7, -5, 2]
total = 0
for n in numbers:
    if n < 0:
        continue
    total += n
    print("Added", n, "running total is", total)
Trace through every value carefully. n is 3: 3 < 0 is False, so continue does not run, total becomes 0 + 3 = 3, and it prints "Added 3 running total is 3". n is -1: -1 < 0 is True, so continue runs, skipping the rest of the body entirely for this particular pass, meaning total is left completely untouched and nothing is printed for -1. n is 7: total becomes 3 + 7 = 10, and that is printed. n is -5: continue skips it again, and total stays at 10. n is 2: total becomes 10 + 2 = 12, and that is printed. After the loop finishes, total is 12, the sum of only the non-negative numbers, because every negative number triggered continue and never actually reached the total += n line at all.

The difference from break is worth stating plainly and remembering well: break stops the loop from running any further passes whatsoever, while continue only cuts the current pass short and trusts the loop to keep going on its own afterward. Both are tools for altering what would otherwise be a straightforward, unconditional run straight through the body every single time.

One thing to watch for in while loops specifically: if the statement that updates your loop's condition sits after the continue in the body, continue will skip that update too, which can accidentally create an infinite loop that never terminates. It is generally safer to place any condition-updating code before a continue, or to structure the loop so that the update happens regardless of which branch actually runs. This is a subtle enough hazard that many programmers deliberately favor for loops with range() whenever continue is involved, since a for loop's advancement to the next item never depends on anything the body does.

Like break, continue is a fine-grained control tool layered on top of the basic idea of loops, letting you shape exactly which parts of the body run on which passes, rather than being stuck accepting an all-or-nothing repetition every time. Both statements exist for the same underlying reason: sometimes the plain "run every line, every pass" behavior of a loop body is not quite what a problem calls for, and Python gives you precise words for the two most common exceptions to that rule.
